questions.question: Think of a car like a house. In the past, you paid for the walls and roof. Now, what part gives the car more value over time?
questions.explanation: According to the text, traditional vehicles have fixed value at the point of sale, while Software-Defined Vehicles continue to develop and generate value over time through software updates and new features.

questions.question: A car gets a new feature after you buy it. How does this happen?
options: The factory builds a new car
questions.explanation: Software-Defined Vehicles improve continuously through Over-the-Air (OTA) updates, which allow new features and performance enhancements to be added without physical modifications or dealership visits.

questions.question: Engineers use a platform for many car models. This is like using the same set of building blocks. Why is this useful?
options: It allows code to work on many cars
questions.explanation: The text emphasizes modular architecture and reusable software as a strategic advantage, enabling engineers to scale and extend capabilities across multiple vehicle lines efficiently.

questions.question: Testing a car in a computer first is like a pilot using a flight simulator. What is the main benefit?
options: It removes the need for sensors
questions.explanation: Simulation and virtual validation enable continuous testing and faster development loops, allowing engineers to identify issues early without waiting for physical hardware to be complete.

questions.question: Imagine you have a recipe you can use for many different meals. Why is this good for car software?
options: It allows the car to drive faster
It helps engineers build new features quickly
questions.explanation: Reusable software components allow engineering teams to rapidly develop and deploy new features without starting from scratch, significantly improving development velocity.

questions.question: Engineers use AI to write test cases. This is like using a smart calculator for math. How does this help?
options: It does all engineering work alone
questions.explanation: The text identifies AI-assisted engineering as a productivity lever that accelerates automated testing and engineering workflows while maintaining human oversight and control.

questions.question: A team buys all the car parts from different shops. The text says this is not enough. Why?
options: Software needs a network of partners to grow
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that SDV cannot be built through procurement alone; it requires a robust engineering ecosystem, strategic partnerships, and long-term capability building.

questions.question: EV sales in Vietnam grew over ten times in a few years. What does this mean for engineers?
options: There is a chance to build new skills and products
questions.explanation: The rapid EV growth in Vietnam signals a strategic opportunity for engineers to participate in the higher-value software and platform layers of the automotive industry.

questions.question: People call cars smartphones on wheels. Why does this idea fail for real cars?
options: Cars must control heavy physics and keep people safe
questions.explanation: The text notes that unlike smartphones, vehicles involve safety-critical physics, strict regulations, cybersecurity risks, and long service lives, requiring a more rigorous engineering approach.

questions.question: A digital-first approach treats a car like a gym membership. What is the main idea?
options: You pay once and use it forever
Value grows over time through services and updates
Hardware is the only thing that matters
questions.explanation: Digital-first design defines vehicle value as a continuous journey, where capabilities improve and generate ongoing revenue through managed software releases and data feedback loops.

questions.question: The SDV stack has clear layers. This is like a house with separate rooms. Why do we need separate layers?
options: To manage risk and ownership for each part
questions.explanation: Each layer in the SDV stack has distinct ownership, release rhythms, and risk profiles, making clear architectural boundaries essential for safe and independent updates.

questions.question: The industry moved from mechanical parts to software. What comes after software in this shift?
questions.explanation: The industry evolution progresses from mechanical-first to electronics-defined, connected, software-defined, and ultimately to digital-first products that continuously improve through data and cloud services.

questions.question: A car uses a camera to check if a child is in the back seat. It gives a warning if the rule is broken. How does this work?
options: It checks rules and warns the driver in real time
questions.explanation: The proposed smart child safety system detects occupancy via in-vehicle cameras, validates compliance with traffic regulations, and provides real-time alerts to the driver.

questions.question: Traditional cars lose value after you buy them. SDV cars gain value later. Why?
options: Software adds new features over time
questions.explanation: While traditional vehicles have fixed value at purchase, SDVs continuously generate new value through OTA updates, AI optimization, and subscription-based feature additions.

questions.question: Car services like safety and navigation are separated from one computer. This is like a power grid. What is the benefit?
options: One part can fail without breaking the whole system
questions.explanation: Decoupling vehicle services from single ECUs allows capabilities to be managed, updated, and isolated independently, improving system reliability and enabling targeted software releases.

questions.question: Cars now use a loop: sense, decide, act, learn, improve. This is like learning a new sport. What is the goal?
options: To make the car better every day using data
questions.explanation: This continuous loop leverages fleet data with proper governance and consent to learn from real-world usage and safely improve vehicle performance and user experience over time.

questions.question: In the SDV stack, each layer has its own release schedule and risk level. Why is this important?
options: It allows safe updates without breaking other parts
questions.explanation: Defining separate release rhythms and risk boundaries per layer ensures that updates can be deployed rapidly and safely without destabilizing other critical vehicle systems.

questions.question: Engineers test features continuously in a virtual space. This is better than testing only after the car is built. Why?
options: It finds errors early and speeds up development
It removes the need for drivers
questions.explanation: Continuous virtual validation accelerates the development cycle by identifying software defects early, reducing dependency on physical prototypes, and enabling faster iteration.

questions.question: AutoNxT wants to lead in SDV. What must they master first?
options: The software layer and system behavior
questions.explanation: The text identifies mastering the software layer, understanding vehicle behavior, and controlling system integration as the foundational capabilities required for long-term SDV leadership.

questions.question: A company buys all the software parts from other firms. Why is this not enough for SDV?
options: SDV requires in-house engineering to integrate and improve features
questions.explanation: The material emphasizes that SDV cannot be achieved through procurement alone; sustainable advantage requires internal engineering capabilities to integrate, customize, and continuously evolve the software stack.
